publishedSummary: The conduction system exists to solve a timing problem: the atria must finish contracting before the ventricles begin, and the ventricles must then be activated almost at once. A fibrous skeleton enforces the first requirement by insulating the chambers, leaving a single controlled route between them.
holdThese: Pacemaker cells show automaticity and rhythmicity — they depolarise spontaneously and regularly.
The fibrous skeleton electrically insulates atrial from ventricular myocardium except through the AV conduction pathway.
AV nodal delay of about 0.1 s lets atrial contraction finish before ventricular contraction begins.
Working myocytes are fast-response cells, depolarising rapidly from about −90 mV once threshold near −65 mV is reached, and are triggered by current from an active neighbour.
Acetylcholine slows the sinoatrial node by lowering cAMP and the funny current; circulating catecholamines speed it by the reverse.
AV block prolongs the PR interval or leaves P waves not followed by QRS complexes.

sections.narrative:
Cardiac cells fall into two electrical classes doing two different jobs. Pacemaker cells show automaticity and rhythmicity: they generate spontaneous, regular action potentials without any external stimulus, because their membrane potential does not rest but drifts steadily upward until it reaches threshold. Automaticity is the capacity to fire unprompted; rhythmicity is the regularity with which they do so.

Working myocytes behave quite differently. A working cardiac myocyte has a stable resting potential near −90 mV and does nothing until something depolarises it to a firing level near −65 mV, at which point it depolarises rapidly — a fast response, driven by fast sodium channels. What provides that depolarisation is not a nerve but the neighbouring muscle: depolarising current from an active neighbouring myocyte, passing through gap junctions, triggers the action potential of a working cardiac myocyte. Cardiac muscle therefore propagates its own activation cell to cell, which is why the myocardium behaves as a functional syncytium and why an impulse arising anywhere in it will eventually spread everywhere it can reach.

The autonomic nervous system does not initiate the heartbeat; it adjusts the rate of the drift in pacemaker cells. Acetylcholine, released by vagal fibres, activates muscarinic receptors in sinoatrial cells and lowers cAMP and the funny current, so the pacemaker potential rises more slowly and threshold is reached later — the heart slows. The sympathetic influence is the mirror image, and it is not purely neural: circulating epinephrine and norepinephrine increase sinoatrial-node firing by mechanisms similar to sympathetic stimulation, raising cAMP and the funny current so that threshold is reached sooner. Because both limbs converge on the same current, the sinoatrial rate at any moment reflects the balance between them.

If cardiac muscle propagates activation freely from cell to cell, something must stop atrial depolarisation from spreading directly into the ventricles — otherwise the two would contract together and filling would be lost. That something is connective tissue. The cardiac fibrous skeleton electrically insulates atrial myocardium from ventricular myocardium except through the atrioventricular conduction pathway. The chambers are separated by a non-conducting ring, and the only electrical route between them is the one the conduction system provides.

That route is deliberately slow. Conduction through the atrioventricular node delays atrial-to-ventricular impulse transmission by about 0.1 second, and the purpose of the delay is straightforward: atrioventricular delay allows atrial contraction to finish before ventricular contraction begins. Without it, the ventricle would start to contract against atria that were still emptying into it. The delay is not a design flaw compensated for elsewhere — it is the mechanism by which the atrial contribution to filling is preserved.

Beyond the node the priority reverses from delay to speed. The atrioventricular bundle passes from the AV node through the fibrous skeleton to reach the interventricular septum, penetrating the insulating ring at the single point where conduction is permitted, then dividing into bundle branches and Purkinje fibres that distribute the impulse rapidly through the ventricular walls so that the ventricular mass contracts as a coordinated unit.

The architecture also defines the failure modes. Because the bundle is the sole crossing point, damage there interrupts everything below it, and because it must pass through the fibrous skeleton close to the aortic and mitral valve rings, disease of those structures can involve it.

Atrioventricular block is impaired impulse conduction from the atria to the ventricles through the atrioventricular conduction system. Since that pathway is the only electrical connection across the fibrous skeleton, anything that slows or interrupts it uncouples the two chambers, and the ECG records the uncoupling directly.

Atrioventricular block may prolong the PR interval or produce P waves that are not followed by QRS complexes. The two findings are the same defect at different severities. The PR interval is the time from the onset of atrial depolarisation to the onset of ventricular depolarisation, and it is dominated by nodal delay; when conduction is merely slowed, that interval lengthens but every impulse still gets through. When conduction fails intermittently, some atrial impulses arrive at ventricles that never respond, and a P wave stands alone with no QRS after it. When it fails completely, no atrial impulse reaches the ventricles at all, and the two chambers beat independently at their own rates.

Read this way, the ECG in AV block is answering one question — how many atrial impulses are reaching the ventricles, and how late — and the classification into degrees is simply a way of recording the answer.
